questions.question: Use 8 + 2 = 10 to work out 8 + 3. Write the answer and tell how the known fact helps.
questions.explanation: Three is one more than two. So 8 + 3 is one more than 8 + 2.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 11 with words or a model showing that 3 is one more than 2, or that one more is added to 10.

questions.question:
17 − __ = 10
Which number is missing?
questions.explanation: Seventeen has 10 and 7. Take away the 7 to leave 10.

questions.question: For 8 + 5, which way of splitting 5 helps you make 10 first?
questions.explanation: Eight needs two to make ten. The other three brings the total to thirteen.

questions.question: Which number-line move shows 16 − 4?
questions.explanation: Subtraction takes away from the starting number. Four steps back from 16 reaches 12.

questions.question: Use 11, 3 and 14 to write an addition equation.
questions.explanation: The two parts, 11 and 3, join to make the whole, 14.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 11 + 3 = 14 or 3 + 11 = 14; reversed equality forms are also valid.

questions.question: To work out 14 − 5, first take away 4 to reach 10. What should you do next?
questions.explanation: Five is four and one. After taking away four, take away one more to get nine.

questions.question:
Choose an easy pair to add first.
4 + 6 + 3 = ?
questions.explanation: Four and six make ten. Add the last three to make thirteen.

questions.question: For 8 + 4, Sam starts at 8 and says “9, 10, 11”. What is missing?
questions.explanation: Sam has counted on only three. One more step reaches 12.

questions.question: The whole is 16. Its parts are 10 and 6. Write two different subtraction equations.
questions.explanation: Subtract either part from the whole to find the other part.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept both 16 − 10 = 6 and 16 − 6 = 10, in either order or with reversed equality.

questions.question: Which calculation also has the answer 7?
questions.explanation: Twelve take away five leaves seven. Counting up from 5 to 12 is another way to check.

questions.question: A card says __ + 4 = 15. Which number belongs in the gap?
questions.explanation: Eleven and four make fifteen. You can find the missing part with 15 − 4.
Taking away all eighteen leaves none. None is written as zero.

questions.question: Make 18 from two different numbers. Both numbers must be greater than 0. Write an addition equation.
questions.explanation: The two chosen parts must total 18. Ten and eight are one possible pair.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept any two different positive whole numbers totalling 18, such as 1 + 17, 2 + 16, 3 + 15, 4 + 14, 5 + 13, 6 + 12, 7 + 11 or 8 + 10, in either order.

questions.question: Start at 9. Jump forward 1 to 10, then forward 6. What is 9 + 7?
questions.explanation: Seven is one and six. The jumps finish at sixteen.

questions.question: 8 + 8 = 16. Which fact has a total one more than 16?
questions.explanation: Only one of the two eights increases by one. The total increases from 16 to 17.

questions.question: Use 6 + 9 = 15. What is 15 − 6?
questions.explanation: Removing one part from the whole leaves the other part, nine.

questions.question: 7 + 7 = 14. Work out 7 + 8 and tell how the double helps.
questions.explanation: Eight is one more than seven, so the total is one more than fourteen.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 15 with an explanation or model showing one extra added to the known double.

questions.question: To work out 16 − 7, take away 6 first. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Sixteen minus six reaches ten. Seven is six and one, so take away one more.

questions.question: The whole is 17. One part is 8. Find the other part.
questions.explanation: Eight and nine make seventeen. The missing part is nine.

questions.question: A row has 11 counters. Five are crossed out. Which equation matches?
questions.explanation: The model starts with eleven and removes five. Six remain.

visual.caption: × crossed-out counter; ● remaining counter.

questions.question: The parts are 5 and 8. The whole is 13. Write one addition equation and one subtraction equation.
questions.explanation: The addition joins the two parts. The subtraction removes one part from the whole.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept either order of 5 + 8 = 13 and either 13 − 5 = 8 or 13 − 8 = 5; reversed equality forms are valid.

questions.question: Lee works out 13 + 4 by saying “13, 14, 15, 16”. What answer should Lee get?
questions.explanation: Do not count the starting number as a step. Four steps after 13 are 14, 15, 16, 17.

questions.question: Compare 5 + 9 and 6 + 8. Which is true?
questions.explanation: Both totals are fourteen. One part gains one while the other loses one.

questions.question:
__ − 4 = 12
What was the starting number?
questions.explanation: Add the removed four back to twelve. The starting number was sixteen.

questions.question: Work out 18 − 9. Show a way to check your answer.
questions.explanation: Nine and nine make eighteen. Removing one nine leaves the other nine.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 9 with a valid check, including 9 + 9 = 18, a counter model, or counting nine steps from 9 to 18.

questions.question: A ten-frame is full. A second ten-frame has 4 counters. Remove those 4 counters. How many remain?
questions.explanation: The full ten-frame stays unchanged. Removing the four extra counters leaves ten.

visual.caption: First two rows: full frame. Last two rows: second frame. × removed; ○ empty.

questions.question: Which addition has the greatest total?
questions.explanation: The totals are 15, 18 and 17. Eighteen is the greatest.

questions.question: Start at 15. Move back 5, then back 3. Where do you finish?
questions.explanation: Fifteen minus five reaches ten. Three more steps back reaches seven.

questions.question: Write a subtraction equation with an answer of 6. Start with a number greater than 10 and no greater than 20.
questions.explanation: Choose a starting number and remove enough to leave six. Fourteen minus eight is one example.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept n − (n−6) = 6 for any whole-number n from 11 to 20, with both numbers shown correctly.

questions.question: Five children are on the mat. Three more join them. Which equation finds how many children are on the mat now?
questions.explanation: The three children join the five already there. Add the two groups to find eight children.

questions.question: A pencil pot holds 12 pencils. Four pencils are taken out. How many stay in the pot?
questions.explanation: The pencils taken out are removed from the starting twelve. Twelve minus four leaves eight.

questions.question: Ana has 7 shells. Ben has 5 shells. How many more shells does Ana have?
questions.explanation: Match five shells from each collection. Ana has two shells left without a match.

visual.caption: Each block represents one shell.

questions.question: There are 6 toy cars on one shelf and 5 on another. Draw a model to show how many cars there are altogether. Write the total.
questions.explanation: Join the group of six and the group of five. Six plus five makes eleven.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept a model with groups of 6 and 5 joined or counted together, with total 11.

questions.question: At a school stall, a sticker costs 15 cents. You pay with a 10-cent coin and a 5-cent coin. How much change should you get?
questions.explanation: Ten cents and five cents total fifteen cents. You paid exactly the price, so there is no change.

questions.question: A pencil costs $2 and a rubber costs $3. How much do they cost altogether?
questions.explanation: Add the two prices: two dollars plus three dollars is five dollars.

questions.question: A tank has some fish. Four more fish are added. Now it has 13 fish. How many fish were there at the start?
questions.explanation: The starting fish and four new fish make thirteen. Take away four from thirteen to find the starting nine.

questions.question: A caterpillar picture needs 12 spots. You have drawn 7 spots. Draw or write a way to find how many more spots it needs.
questions.explanation: Count on from seven to twelve, or subtract seven from twelve. Five spots are still needed.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 5 more spots with 7 + 5 = 12, 12 − 7 = 5, a labelled gap model, or a drawing showing 7 existing and 5 additional spots.

questions.question: There are 18 counters in a bag. Five are taken out. Which model matches the story?

options.A: 13 at the start; add 5; 18 at the end.
options.B: 5 at the start; remove 5; 0 at the end.
options.C: 18 at the start; remove 5; 13 at the end.

questions.answer: 18 at the start; remove 5; 13 at the end.
questions.explanation: The story starts with eighteen and removes five. The model must leave thirteen in the bag.

questions.question: A book costs $6. You pay with a $10 note. How much change should you get?
questions.explanation: Six dollars for the book and four dollars in change make the ten dollars paid.

questions.question: Max has 6 toy animals. Liv has 2 fewer than Max. How many toy animals does Liv have?
questions.explanation: Two fewer than six means taking away two. Liv has four toy animals.

questions.question: Make a short story that matches 8 − 3 = 5. Tell what the 8, the 3 and the 5 mean.
questions.answer: There were 8 balloons. Three burst. Five balloons were left.
questions.explanation: Eight minus three is five. A matching story can remove three from eight, compare eight and three, or find the missing part of eight.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept any sensible story or labelled drawing representing 8 − 3 = 5, including taking away 3 from 8, comparing amounts of 8 and 3 to find a difference of 5, or finding the missing part of 8 when the known part is 3. The roles of all three numbers must be clear.
questions.correct_answer: There were 8 balloons. Three burst. Five balloons were left.

questions.question: Ten books are on a table. Some are put on a shelf. Four books stay on the table. Which equation helps find how many were moved?
questions.explanation: The ten books split into books moved and books left. Taking away the four left finds the six moved.
questions.question_type: Choose an equation for a missing change

questions.question: A toy costs $7. Which payment is exactly $7?
questions.explanation: Five dollars and two dollars make seven dollars. This payment matches the price.

questions.question: The red team has 9 points. The blue team has 6 points. How many points does the blue team need to catch up?
questions.explanation: The blue team needs the gap between six and nine. Three more points makes the scores equal.
questions.question_type: Find an amount needed to match

questions.question:
Complete the story with an equation.
Blocks in the box at first: 9
Blocks added: 6
Blocks in the box at the end: ?
questions.explanation: Six blocks join the nine already in the box. The new total is fifteen blocks.
questions.question_type: Turn a start-change table into an equation
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 9 + 6 = 15 or 6 + 9 = 15, including reversed equality.

questions.question: A tray has 6 red beads, 4 blue beads and 2 green beads. How many red and blue beads are there altogether?
questions.explanation: Only the red and blue beads are wanted. Add six and four to get ten.
questions.question_type: Select quantities needed for a model

questions.question: A box has 12 blocks. You want it to have 9 blocks. What should you do?
questions.explanation: Twelve is three more than nine. Removing three leaves the nine blocks wanted.
questions.question_type: Choose an action to reach a target

questions.question: A cup costs $4. A plate costs $5. The price tag for both says $10. What should the total price be?
questions.explanation: The two prices add to nine dollars. The ten-dollar tag is one dollar too much.

questions.question: At a class shop, a card costs 15 cents. You pay 20 cents. Write the change and an equation to check it.
questions.explanation: Fifteen cents and five cents make the twenty cents paid. So the change is five cents.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 5 cents with 15 + 5 = 20 or 20 − 15 = 5, with cents stated or clear from the response.

questions.question: A bowl had 14 cherries. After snack time, 9 cherries were left. How many cherries were eaten?
questions.explanation: The eaten cherries and the nine left make fourteen. Fourteen minus nine gives five eaten.

questions.question: A bus has 7 occupied seats and 5 empty seats. Which drawing plan would show the total number of seats?

options.C: Draw 7 occupied seats and 5 more empty seats.

questions.answer: Draw 7 occupied seats and 5 more empty seats.
questions.explanation: Occupied and empty seats are the two parts of all the seats. Drawing both parts shows the total of twelve.

questions.question: You have $8 and spend $5 on a snack. Which item can you buy with exactly the money left?
questions.explanation: Eight dollars minus five dollars leaves three dollars. The badge costs exactly that amount.
questions.question_type: Use a remaining amount to select a purchase

questions.question: A small ball costs $3. A kite costs $8. Show their total cost with a drawing or an equation.
questions.explanation: Join the two prices to find the cost of both items. Three dollars and eight dollars make eleven dollars.
questions.question_type: Create a model for combined purchases
questions.acceptance_note: Accept total $11 with 3 + 8 = 11, 8 + 3 = 11, or a clear labelled money model.

questions.question: A class puts 12 paintings on a wall, then adds 5 more. How many paintings are on the wall now?
questions.explanation: The five new paintings join the first twelve. Twelve plus five makes seventeen.

questions.question: A shelf had 16 cups. Some cups were taken away. Eleven cups remain. Which equation puts the cups taken away in the gap?
questions.explanation: The story gives the starting sixteen and the remaining eleven. The blank is the number taken away, five.

questions.question: A puzzle costs $7. You pay with a $10 note. How much change should you receive?
questions.explanation: Seven dollars for the puzzle and three dollars in change make ten dollars.

questions.question: Thirteen children each need a ticket. Seven tickets are ready. Show how to find the number of extra tickets needed.
questions.explanation: The seven ready tickets and six extra tickets make thirteen.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 6 extra tickets with 13 − 7 = 6, 7 + 6 = 13, counting on, or a matching model.

questions.question: Two towers use the same-size blocks. One tower has 8 blocks. The other has 12 blocks. How many blocks taller is the second tower?
questions.explanation: Match the first eight blocks in both towers. Four blocks remain above the shorter tower.

visual.caption: Each block represents one building block. All building blocks are the same size.

questions.question: A bag costs $6 and a hat costs $8. What is the cost of buying both?
questions.explanation: Both prices are parts of the total. Six dollars plus eight dollars is fourteen dollars.

questions.question: There are 9 spoons and 6 bowls. Each bowl needs one spoon. Which equation finds the extra spoons?
questions.explanation: Pair one spoon with each of the six bowls. Subtract six from nine to find the three extra spoons.

questions.question: Six toy boats were taken from a box. Seven boats were left. Draw a model or write an equation to find how many boats were in the box at first.
questions.explanation: The boats removed and the boats left are the two parts of the starting amount. Together they make thirteen.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 13 boats with 6 + 7 = 13, 7 + 6 = 13, 13 − 6 = 7, or a drawing showing both parts.

questions.question: A game costs $5. You pay with two $2 coins and one $1 coin. Which is true?
questions.explanation: Two dollars plus two dollars plus one dollar makes five dollars. The payment matches the price.
questions.question_type: Check a payment made from several coins

questions.question: Fifteen paint pots each need a lid. There are only 9 lids. How many more lids are needed?
questions.explanation: Nine lids are already available. Six more will make fifteen lids, one for every pot.
questions.question_type: Find an amount needed to match

questions.question: A basket has 4 bread rolls. Seven more are added. Jo says there are 3 rolls now. What is the correct total?
questions.explanation: More rolls were added, so join the quantities. Four plus seven is eleven.
questions.question_type: Correct an operation chosen for a story

questions.question: You have 20 cents. You spend 5 cents at a class shop. Write an equation showing how much money is left.
questions.explanation: Spending five cents removes five from twenty. Fifteen cents remain.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 20 − 5 = 15, or 5 + 15 = 20 with 15 cents identified as the amount left.

questions.question: A stamp at a school stall costs 15 cents. You have a 10-cent coin. Which extra coin lets you pay exactly?
questions.explanation: Ten cents and five cents make fifteen cents. The five-cent coin fills the gap.
questions.question_type: Find a coin needed to complete payment

questions.question: There are 17 books to pack. A box already holds 10 of them. How many books still need packing?
questions.explanation: The packed books and unpacked books make seventeen. Taking away the ten packed books leaves seven.
questions.question_type: Find an uncompleted part of a task

questions.question: A tub has 14 balls. Four are taken out. Then 2 are put back. How many balls are in the tub now?
questions.explanation: Four taken from fourteen leaves ten. Putting two back brings the total to twelve.

questions.question: A shop sells a pen for $4, a notebook for $6 and a folder for $7. Choose two different items that cost exactly $10 altogether. Show your choice with an equation.
questions.explanation: Four dollars and six dollars make ten dollars. The other pairs cost more than ten dollars.
questions.question_type: Create a purchase within an exact budget
questions.acceptance_note: Accept pen and notebook with 4 + 6 = 10 or 6 + 4 = 10; item names may be labels on a clear model.

questions.question: Share 6 counters equally between 3 children. How many counters does each child get?
questions.explanation: Give one counter to each child, then one more to each. Each child gets two.
questions.question_type: Find a share by equal distribution

questions.question: Put 8 blocks into groups of 2. How many groups can you make?
questions.explanation: Make pairs until all eight blocks are used. There are four pairs.
questions.question_type: Find the number of equal groups

questions.question: Six beads are shared among 3 children. Which list shows equal shares?
questions.explanation: Equal shares have the same number for every child. Three shares of two use all six beads.

questions.question: Draw 4 plates. Share 12 cherries equally onto them. Write how many cherries are on each plate.
questions.explanation: Give each plate one cherry at a time. Twelve cherries make four equal shares of three.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept four groups of three with 3 identified as the number on each plate.

questions.question: There are 12 counters. Put 3 counters in each group. Which model follows the rule and uses all the counters?
questions.explanation: The rule fixes three counters in every group. Four groups of three use all twelve counters.
questions.question_type: Choose a model for a fixed group size

questions.question:
Fifteen beads are shared equally among 3 children. Complete the table.
Children: 3
Beads altogether: 15
Beads for each child: ?
questions.explanation: Deal the beads equally to the three children. Each child gets five, using all fifteen.

questions.question: Two plates have 7 and 3 grapes. Move grapes from the first plate to make the shares equal. How many grapes should you move?
questions.explanation: Move two grapes from the plate with seven to the plate with three. Both plates will then have five.
questions.question_type: Repair unequal shares by moving objects

questions.question: Draw 14 counters. Ring every pair. How many pairs will there be?
questions.explanation: Count the counters in twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. There are seven pairs.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept a drawing of seven pairs with two counters in each, and a pair count of 7.

questions.question: Three bowls each hold 4 berries. The groups are [4], [4], [4]. How many berries are there altogether?
questions.explanation: Count the equal groups: four, eight, twelve. There are twelve berries altogether.
questions.question_type: Find a total from equal groups

questions.question: Three children each have 2 counters. There are 3 counters still to share. Give one more to each child. How many counters does each child have now?
questions.explanation: Each child starts with two and receives one more. The equal shares become three each.

questions.question: Ten crackers must be shared equally between 2 plates. Which plan is correct?

options.A: Put 2 crackers on each of 5 plates.

questions.explanation: The number of plates is fixed at two. Five crackers on each uses all ten equally.
questions.question_type: Distinguish shares from number of groups

questions.question: Make equal groups with 8 counters. Use more than one group and more than one counter in every group. Draw one way.
questions.explanation: Two groups of four use all eight equally. Four groups of two also work.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept exactly two groups of four or four groups of two; all eight counters must be used.

questions.question: The beads are grouped like this: [3], [3], [3], [3]. How many groups are there?
questions.explanation: Count the groups, not the beads inside each group. There are four groups.
questions.question_type: Distinguish the group count from the total

questions.question: One child has 4 counters in a row. Another has 4 counters arranged in two pairs. Are the shares equal?

options.B: No, two pairs is only 2 counters.

questions.explanation: The arrangement does not change the number. Two pairs contain four counters, just like the row.
questions.question_type: Check equal shares in different arrangements

questions.question: Put 15 pencils into packs of 5. How many full packs can you make?
questions.explanation: Use five pencils in the first pack, five in the second and five in the third. All fifteen are packed.

questions.question: Twenty cards go into packs of 5. Draw or describe the packs. How many packs are there?
questions.explanation: Five, ten, fifteen, twenty counts four equal packs.
questions.question_type: Represent grouping in a packing task
questions.acceptance_note: Accept four groups of five, a labelled drawing, or a description stating 4 packs with 5 cards each.

questions.question: Share all 16 counters equally between 2 children. Which result is correct?
questions.explanation: Eight counters for each child uses sixteen altogether. Both children have the same amount and all counters are used.
questions.question_type: Check that an equal share uses the whole

questions.question: Three bags hold 3, 3 and 2 marbles. You may add marbles to the last bag. How many should you add to make all the bags equal?
questions.explanation: The first two bags each have three. Add one to the bag with two so it also has three.

questions.question: You have 12 counters. Which sharing plan gives each child more counters?

options.A: Both plans give the same share.

questions.explanation: Two children get six each. Three children get four each, so sharing between two gives the larger share.
questions.question_type: Compare shares for a fixed total

questions.question: Four hoops each hold 3 beanbags. Write the number of groups and the number in each group.
questions.explanation: Each hoop is one group. There are four hoops, and each contains three beanbags.
questions.question_type: Label the parts of an equal-group model
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 4 groups and 3 in each, with the roles correctly identified.

questions.question: Twelve flowers are shared equally among 3 vases. Two vases each show 4 flowers. How many are in the covered vase?
questions.explanation: Equal shares mean the covered vase has the same as each other vase. Four flowers in each vase uses twelve.

questions.question: A pair of mittens has 2 mittens. How many pairs can you make from 6 mittens?
questions.explanation: Match the six mittens into groups of two. There are three pairs.
questions.question_type: Interpret a pair as a group

questions.question: You have 18 blocks and want 3 equal groups. How many blocks should go in each group?
questions.explanation: Deal all eighteen blocks into three groups. Each group has six.
questions.question_type: Choose a group size for a fixed group count

questions.question: There are 12 counters. Draw two different ways to put them into equal groups. Use at least 2 groups in each way.
questions.answer: Two groups of six; three groups of four.
questions.explanation: The number of counters stays twelve, but the group sizes can change. Every group in one drawing must be equal.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept any two distinct arrangements using all 12: 2 groups of 6, 3 of 4, 4 of 3, 6 of 2, or 12 of 1. Swapping group positions is not a different arrangement.
questions.correct_answer: Two groups of six; three groups of four.

questions.question: Share 16 stickers equally among 4 children. How many stickers does each child get?
questions.explanation: Deal one sticker to every child in turn. Each child receives four stickers.
questions.question_type: Find a share by equal distribution

questions.question: There are 18 counters. Put 3 counters in each group. How many groups are there?
questions.explanation: Count groups of three until all eighteen are used. Six equal groups are made.
questions.question_type: Find the number of equal groups

questions.question: Twelve berries are shared among 3 bowls. Which list shows equal shares using all the berries?
questions.explanation: All three bowls must have the same number. Four in each bowl uses twelve berries.

questions.question: Use 10 dots to draw pairs. Write how many pairs you made.
questions.explanation: Each pair uses two dots. Five pairs use all ten dots.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept a drawing of five groups of two dots and a pair count of 5.

questions.question: One plate has 9 counters. The other has 5. How many counters must move from the first plate to the second to make equal shares?
questions.explanation: Moving two changes the shares to seven and seven. Both plates then have equal numbers.
questions.question_type: Repair unequal shares by moving objects

questions.question: There are 4 equal groups with 5 buttons in each. How many buttons are there altogether?
questions.explanation: Count the four groups: five, ten, fifteen, twenty.
questions.question_type: Find a total from an equal-group table

questions.question: Four bags each hold 5 pebbles. Take 1 pebble from every bag. How many pebbles are in each bag now?
questions.explanation: Every group loses the same amount. Five minus one leaves four pebbles in each bag.

questions.question: Three plates have 3, 3 and 6 counters. Move counters to make three equal shares. Describe what to move.
questions.answer: Move one counter from the plate with 6 to each plate with 3.
questions.explanation: There are twelve counters in all, so each plate needs four. Moving one to each smaller share makes four on every plate.
questions.question_type: Design a repair for unequal shares
questions.acceptance_note: Accept a clear sequence of moves or a final model with 4 counters on each plate, using all 12 counters.
questions.correct_answer: Move one counter from the plate with 6 to each plate with 3.

questions.question: Use all 18 beads. Put 6 beads on each string. Which model is correct?
questions.explanation: The rule says six beads per string. Three such strings use all eighteen beads.
questions.question_type: Choose a model for a fixed group size

questions.question: One child has 6 counters close together. Another has 6 counters spread out. Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Each child has six counters. Moving the counters farther apart does not change the share.

questions.question: Ten toy people stand in groups of 2. A child says, “There are 2 groups.” What is the correct number of groups?
questions.explanation: Two is the number in each group. Ten toy people make five groups of two.

questions.question: Share 20 counters equally among 4 cups. Draw the shares or describe them. How many are in each cup?
questions.explanation: Give the same number to each of the four cups. Five in every cup uses all twenty.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept four groups of five, with 5 identified as the number in each cup.

questions.question: Sixteen blocks are grouped as [4], [4], [4], [4]. Which sentence matches?

options.A: There are 4 groups with 16 in each.
options.B: There are 16 groups with 4 in each.
options.C: There are 4 groups with 4 in each.

questions.answer: There are 4 groups with 4 in each.
questions.explanation: Count four groups. Each one contains four blocks.
questions.question_type: Interpret the roles in an equal-group model

questions.question: Share 8 counters equally. Which plan gives each child fewer counters?

options.C: Both plans give the same share.

questions.explanation: Two children would get four each. Four children would get two each, which is a smaller share.
questions.question_type: Compare shares for a fixed total

questions.question: Two baskets each hold 5 apples. You have 5 more apples and put them in another basket. How many equal baskets of 5 are there now?
questions.explanation: The five extra apples make one new group of five. Two groups and one new group make three equal groups.

questions.question: Draw equal groups using 18 counters, with 6 counters in every group. Label the number of groups and the number in each group.
questions.explanation: Three groups of six use all eighteen counters. The group count is three and the group size is six.
questions.question_type: Create and label a grouping solution
questions.acceptance_note: Accept exactly three groups of six and correct labels for 3 groups and 6 in each.

questions.question:
Look at the growing rows.
Row 1: ■ ■
Row 2: ■ ■ ■ ■
Row 3: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■
How many squares are added each time?
questions.explanation: The rows have 2, 4 and 6 squares. Each new row has 2 more squares.

questions.question:
Count on by 5.
10, 15, __, 25
Which number is missing?
questions.explanation: Add 5 each time: 10, 15, 20, 25.

questions.question:
Each new row of a sticker chart has 10 more stickers than the row before it.
Row | Stickers
1 | 10
2 | 20
3 | ?
How many stickers are in row 3?
questions.explanation: The numbers of stickers go up by 10: 10, 20, 30.

questions.question:
Start at 6. Count on by 2.
Write the next two numbers.
6, __, __
questions.explanation: Add 2 to 6 to get 8. Add 2 again to get 10.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 8 and 10 in that order; separators do not matter.

questions.question: Which row counts on by 10 each time?
questions.explanation: In 10, 20, 30, 40, every step adds 10.

questions.question:
Each new picture has 2 more stars.
Picture 1: ★ ★
Picture 2: ★ ★ ★ ★
Picture 3: ?
Which row belongs in picture 3?
questions.explanation: Picture 2 has 4 stars. Add 2 stars to make 6 stars.

questions.question:
A path has labels that count on by 5.
5 → 10 → 15 → ?
Which label comes next?
questions.explanation: Five more than 15 is 20. The path labels are 5, 10, 15, 20.

questions.question:
Make a number pattern. Start at 0 and count on by 5.
Write the next three numbers.
0, __, __, __
questions.explanation: Adding 5 each time makes 0, 5, 10, 15.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 5, 10, 15 in that order.

questions.question:
This should count on by 5.
5, 10, 12, 20
Which number should replace 12?
questions.explanation: Counting by 5 gives 5, 10, 15, 20.

questions.question:
Look at the growing rows of dots.
Row 1: ● ● ●
Row 2: ● ● ● ● ●
Row 3: ● ● ● ● ● ● ●
Which number pattern matches the rows?
questions.explanation: There are 3 dots, then 5 dots, then 7 dots. The pattern adds 2 dots each time.

questions.question:
Start at 30. Count on by 10 two times.
30 → __ → ?
Which number goes at the question mark?
questions.explanation: Count 30, 40, 50. Two steps of 10 reach 50.

questions.question:
The bead rows grow by 2 each time.
Row | Beads
1 | 2
2 | 4
3 | 6
4 | __
Write the number of beads in row 4.
questions.explanation: The bead counts are 2, 4, 6, 8. Add 2 to 6.

questions.question:
Look at the numbers.
10, 15, 20, 25
What is the counting rule?
questions.explanation: Each number is 5 more than the number before it.

questions.question:
A strip grows by one group of 5 dots each time.
Strip 1: one group of 5
Strip 2: two groups of 5
Strip 3: three groups of 5
Which number pattern gives the totals?
questions.explanation: One group has 5 dots. Counting the growing totals by 5 gives 5, 10, 15.

questions.question:
Count on by 10.
10, 20, __, 40, __
Which pair fills the gaps in order?
questions.explanation: The whole pattern is 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.

questions.question:
Count on by 2. Fill both gaps.
16, __, __, 22
questions.explanation: Counting on by 2 gives 16, 18, 20, 22.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 18 and 20 in that order.

questions.question:
Start at 7 and count on by 2.
Which pattern is right?
questions.explanation: Add 2 each time, even when the starting number is 7.

questions.question:
Each new picture has 5 more dots.
Picture 1 has 5 dots.
Picture 2 has 10 dots.
A child says picture 3 has 11 dots.
Is the child right?
questions.explanation: This pattern adds 5, not 1. Five more than 10 is 15.

questions.question:
Two patterns start at 0.
A: 0, 2, 4, 6
B: 0, 5, 10, 15
Which pattern adds 5 at every step?
questions.explanation: Pattern B adds 5 each time. Pattern A adds 2 each time.

questions.question:
Make the next row by adding 2 squares each time.
Row 1: ■
Row 2: ■ ■ ■
Row 3: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■
Draw or write the squares for row 4.
questions.explanation: The rows have 1, 3 and 5 squares. The next row has 7 squares.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept a row of seven squares or seven clearly drawn identical shapes. A bare 7 identifies the total but does not create the requested row.

questions.question:
Count on by 10 from 20.
20, 30, 40, ...
Which number will appear later in this pattern?
questions.explanation: Continuing gives 50, 60, 70. The pattern reaches 60.

questions.question:
The number pattern is 2, 4, 6.
Which set of rows matches it?
questions.explanation: The matching rows have 2, 4 and 6 dots. Each row adds 2 dots.

questions.question:
Look at the patterns.
A: 2, 4, 6, 8
B: 3, 5, 7, 9
Do they use the same counting step?

options.C: No, A adds 2 and B adds 3

questions.explanation: Both patterns add 2 between neighbouring numbers. They can start at different numbers.

questions.question:
Make your own pattern of four numbers that counts on by 10.
Start at 0, 10 or 20.
questions.explanation: Choose an allowed starting number and add 10 three times. One pattern is 20, 30, 40, 50.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept exactly four numbers starting at 0, 10 or 20, with 10 added at each step. Other valid answers are 0,10,20,30 and 10,20,30,40.

questions.question:
The dot rows grow.
Row 1: ●
Row 2: ● ● ●
Row 3: ● ● ● ● ●
What is added to make each new row?
questions.explanation: The counts are 1, 3 and 5. Each row adds 2 dots.

questions.question:
Count on by 5 from 20.
20, __, __
Which pair comes next?
questions.explanation: Add 5 each time: 20, 25, 30.

questions.question:
The tower heights grow by 10 blocks each time.
Tower | Blocks
A | 10
B | 20
C | ?
D | 40
How many blocks are in tower C?
questions.explanation: The heights follow 10, 20, 30, 40. The missing height is 30 blocks.

questions.question:
Create a pattern. Start at 11 and count on by 2.
Write the next three numbers.
11, __, __, __
questions.explanation: Add 2 each time to get 11, 13, 15, 17.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 13, 15 and 17 in that order.

questions.question:
A row grows by 2 squares each time.
Row 1: ■ ■
Row 2: ■ ■ ■ ■
Row 3: ■ ■ ■ ■ ■ ■
How many squares are in row 4?
questions.explanation: The square counts are 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.question:
This pattern should count on by 10.
20, 30, 41, 50
Which number should replace 41?
questions.explanation: The correct pattern is 20, 30, 40, 50.

questions.question:
These numbers count on by 5.
__, 10, 15, 20
Which number starts the pattern?
questions.explanation: Starting at 5 gives 5, 10, 15, 20 when you count on by 5.

questions.question:
The rows grow by 2 dots each time.
Row 1: ● ● ●
Row 2: ● ● ● ● ●
Draw or write the dots for row 3.
questions.explanation: Add 2 dots to the 5 dots in row 2. Row 3 has 7 dots.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept seven dots or seven clearly drawn identical shapes. A bare 7 identifies the total but does not create the requested row.

questions.question: Which picture counts follow the rule “add 5”?
questions.explanation: Both steps in 5, 10, 15 add 5.

questions.question:
A trail has labels that count on by 2.
12 → 14 → 16 → ?
Which label is missing?
questions.explanation: Two more than 16 is 18.

questions.question:
Pattern A: 10, 20, 30
Pattern B: 10, 15, 20
Which statement is right?
questions.explanation: The steps in A are 10. The steps in B are 5.

questions.question:
Each new row of a token display has 5 more tokens.
Row | Tokens
1 | 5
2 | 10
3 | 15
4 | __
Write the missing total.
questions.explanation: The totals go 5, 10, 15, 20.

questions.question:
Start at 40. Count on by 10.
40, 50, ...
Which number will appear later?
questions.explanation: Continuing the pattern gives 60, 70, 80.

questions.question:
The rows have these numbers of triangles:
2, 4, 6, 8
A new row is made by adding 2 triangles.
Which number sentence matches the next step?
questions.explanation: The pattern adds 2 each time, so the next row has 10 triangles.

questions.question:
A child continues this pattern by adding 5.
5, 10, 15, ...
Which next pair follows the rule?
questions.explanation: Five more than 15 is 20, and five more than 20 is 25.

questions.question:
Make a pattern of four numbers that counts on by 5.
Start at 0, 5 or 10.
questions.explanation: Choose an allowed starting number and keep adding 5. One answer is 10, 15, 20, 25.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept four numbers starting at 0, 5 or 10 with 5 added at each step. Other valid answers are 0,5,10,15 and 5,10,15,20.

questions.question:
The shapes repeat.
● ▲ ● ▲ ● __
Which shape comes next?
questions.explanation: The unit ● ▲ repeats. After ● comes ▲.

questions.question:
Look at the repeating pattern.
■ ● ▲ ■ ● ▲ ■ ● ▲
What is the smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The three-shape unit ■ ● ▲ is repeated in the same order.

questions.question:
Fill the gap in this repeating pattern.
■ ■ ● ■ ■ __ ■ ■ ●
questions.explanation: The unit is ■ ■ ●. The gap completes the middle unit.

questions.question:
The actions repeat.
clap, tap, clap, tap, __, __
Write the next two actions.
questions.explanation: The repeating unit is clap, tap. Repeat that unit again.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept clap then tap, written or demonstrated in that order.

questions.question:
The pattern repeats this unit: ▲ ● ●.
▲ ● ● | ▲ ● ● | __
Which whole unit comes next?
questions.explanation: Repeat the whole unit ▲ ● ● in the same order.

questions.question:
The pattern should repeat ▲ ■.
▲ ■ ▲ ● ▲ ■
Which shape should replace ●?
questions.explanation: Each ▲ should be followed by ■. Replacing ● with ■ repairs the pattern.

questions.question:
The numbers repeat.
1, 2, 1, 2, 1, __
Which number comes next?
questions.explanation: The repeating unit is 1, 2. After 1 comes 2.

questions.question:
Use this repeating unit: ■ ■ ●.
Draw or write the unit three times in a row.
questions.explanation: Each unit has two squares and then one circle. Three units make nine shapes.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept exactly three consecutive copies of square, square, circle; separators between units are optional.

questions.question:
The actions repeat.
hop, hop, clap, hop, hop, clap
Which action happens twice in each smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The smallest unit is hop, hop, clap. It has two hops and one clap.

questions.question:
The shapes repeat one of each kind.
● ▲ ● ▲
Which object pattern works the same way?
questions.explanation: Both patterns repeat one item of each kind in turn.

questions.question:
The pattern repeats.
▲ ● ■ ▲ __ ■ ▲ ● ■
Which shape fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The unit ▲ ● ■ repeats. The missing middle shape is ●.

questions.question:
Look at the repeating numbers.
4, 4, 7, 4, 4, 7, 4, 4, 7
Write the smallest repeating unit.
questions.explanation: The group 4, 4, 7 repeats three times.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 4, 4, 7 in that order. Do not accept the larger six- or nine-number group when asked for the smallest unit.

questions.question:
Look at the number pattern.
2, 5, 2, 5, 2, 5
Which rule makes it?
questions.explanation: The same pair 2, 5 appears again and again. The numbers do not keep getting bigger.

questions.question:
The shapes repeat ▲ ● ■.
▲ ● ■ ▲ ● __ __
Which two shapes fill the gaps in order?
questions.explanation: Finish the current unit with ■. Then start the next unit with ▲.

questions.question:
The repeating unit is ● ● ▲.
Which row uses it correctly?
questions.explanation: The correct row repeats two circles followed by one triangle.

questions.question:
Make an action pattern like this shape pattern.
■ ● ● | ■ ● ●
Use “stamp” for ■ and “clap” for ●.
Write or show all six actions.
questions.answer: stamp, clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap
questions.explanation: Each square becomes a stamp and each circle becomes a clap. The unit stamp, clap, clap repeats twice.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept stamp, clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap in order, written or demonstrated.
questions.correct_answer: stamp, clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap

questions.question:
Look at this repeating unit: ▲ ■ ■.
Which row shows the unit three times?
questions.explanation: Repeat ▲ ■ ■ three times without changing the order.

questions.question:
A line of objects repeats.
hat, shoe, sock, hat, shoe, sock, __
Which object comes next?
questions.explanation: The unit hat, shoe, sock starts again after sock.

questions.question:
A row repeats this unit: cup, cup, plate.
cup, cup, plate | ? | cup, cup, plate
Which group belongs at the question mark?
questions.explanation: The missing group must be the same whole unit: cup, cup, plate.

questions.question:
Choose two different shapes. Make a repeating pattern with one of each shape in its unit.
Show the unit three times.
questions.explanation: Choose a two-shape unit, such as ● ▲, and repeat it three times.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept any six-shape ABABAB pattern with A and B different, including clearly drawn shapes or written shape names.

questions.question:
Look at the pattern.
3, 6, 3, 6, 3, 6
Which group can repeat to make the whole pattern?
questions.explanation: Repeating 3, 6 makes 3, 6, 3, 6, 3, 6. Repeating 3, 6, 3 would put two 3s together.

questions.question:
The shapes repeat.
● ● ▲ ■ | ● ● ▲ ■
How many shapes are in the smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The unit ● ● ▲ ■ has four shapes. The two circles both belong to the unit.

questions.question: Which number row repeats the unit 2, 4?
questions.explanation: The row 2, 4, 2, 4 shows the unit 2, 4 twice.

questions.question:
The pattern repeats two squares, then two circles.
■ ■ ● ● | ■ ■ ● ● | __ __ __ __
Draw or write the next four shapes.
questions.explanation: Repeat the unit ■ ■ ● ● to continue the pattern.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept square, square, circle, circle in order, written or drawn.

questions.question:
The objects repeat.
leaf, stone, leaf, stone, leaf, __
Which object comes next?
questions.explanation: The unit leaf, stone repeats. After leaf comes stone.

questions.question:
Look at the repeating shapes.
● ■ ■ ● ■ ■ ● ■ ■
What is the smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The unit has one circle and then two squares.

questions.question:
The numbers repeat.
5, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0, 5, __, 0
Which number fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The unit is 5, 0, 0. The missing number is the first 0 in the last unit.

questions.question:
Look at the repeating pattern.
★ ● ▲ ★ ● ▲ ★ ● ▲
Draw or write the smallest repeating unit.
questions.explanation: The unit star, circle, triangle repeats three times.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept star, circle, triangle in that order, drawn or written; require the three-shape smallest unit.

questions.question:
The shapes repeat.
● ■ ■ ▲ ● ■ __ ▲
Which shape fills the gap?
questions.explanation: The unit is ● ■ ■ ▲. The second unit also needs two squares.

questions.question:
These actions repeat: clap, stamp, clap, stamp.
Which pattern has the same one-of-each structure?
questions.explanation: Both patterns repeat one action and then a different action.

questions.question:
The pattern repeats ★ ● ▲.
★ ● ▲ ★ __ __
Which two shapes fill the gaps in order?
questions.explanation: After the star, finish the unit with a circle and a triangle.

questions.question:
Use this repeating unit: 2, 2, 5.
Write a pattern that shows the unit three times.
questions.explanation: Keep the order 2, 2, 5 each time you repeat the unit.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept exactly three consecutive copies of 2, 2, 5; separators are optional.

questions.question:
Look at the repeating pattern.
▲ ● ▲ ● ▲ ● ▲ ●
Which is its smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The pair ▲ ● is enough to repeat and make the whole pattern. The four-shape group is a larger repeated group.

questions.question:
A border repeats this unit: ■ ● ●.
The border so far is: ■ ● ● | ■ ● ●
Which change keeps that same unit?
questions.explanation: Adding another complete ■ ● ● unit keeps the pattern repeating correctly.

questions.question:
The pattern should repeat 8, 1.
8, 1, 8, 8, 8, 1
Which number should replace the fourth number?
questions.explanation: The correct pattern is 8, 1, 8, 1, 8, 1.

questions.question:
Make a repeating pattern using “tap, clap, clap” as the unit.
Write or show the unit two times.
questions.answer: tap, clap, clap, tap, clap, clap
questions.explanation: The complete three-action unit repeats twice.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept tap, clap, clap, tap, clap, clap in order, written or demonstrated.
questions.correct_answer: tap, clap, clap, tap, clap, clap

questions.question:
The row repeats: shell, shell, stone, shell, shell, stone.
How many objects are in the smallest repeating unit?
questions.explanation: The unit shell, shell, stone contains three objects.

questions.question:
The pattern repeats ● ● ▲.
● ● ▲ ● ● ▲ ● __ __
Which pair fills the gaps in order?
questions.explanation: The last unit has its first circle. It still needs one circle and one triangle.

questions.question:
A pattern repeats the unit 1, 3, 3.
Which row follows the rule?
questions.explanation: Repeat all three numbers in order: 1, 3, 3.

questions.question:
Choose two different shapes. Make a repeating unit with two of the first shape, then one of the second shape.
Show your unit two times.
questions.explanation: One possible unit is square, square, circle. Repeating it twice gives ■ ■ ● ■ ■ ●.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept any six-shape AABAAB pattern with A and B different, drawn or written as shape names.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two strips start at the same place. Strip A ends before strip B. Which strip is longer?
questions.explanation: From the same starting point, the strip that reaches further is longer.

visual.caption: Both objects start at the same place. Each block is the same length.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A balance has a stone on one side and a shell on the other. The stone side goes down. Which is heavier?
questions.explanation: The heavier side of a balance goes down.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Cup A is full of water. All its water is poured into empty cup B. Cup B is not full yet. Which cup holds more when full?
questions.explanation: Cup B holds all the water from A and still has room for more.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two toy cars start moving together. Car A stops first. Car B keeps moving. Which car moves for a longer time?
questions.explanation: Car B keeps moving after car A stops.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept B or car B.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A card is shorter than a pencil. A bookmark is longer than the same pencil. Which is longer: the card or the bookmark?
questions.explanation: The card is shorter than the pencil, but the bookmark is longer than it. So the bookmark is longer than the card.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A lunch box is lighter than a bag. The bag is lighter than a basket. Which order goes from lightest to heaviest?
questions.explanation: The lunch box is lightest. The basket is heaviest.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question:
Fill each container using the same little cup.
Jug: 5 cupfuls
Bottle: 3 cupfuls
Which holds more?
questions.explanation: The jug takes more of the same cupfuls to fill.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Jo and Sam start together. Jo finishes a puzzle first. Sam finishes a drawing later. Which activity took less time?
questions.explanation: The puzzle finished first when both activities had the same start.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept puzzle, Jo, or Jo’s puzzle.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two pencils have their tips lined up. Their other ends also line up. What is true?
questions.explanation: Matching both ends shows that the pencils have equal lengths.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A big empty box and a small stone sit on a balance. The balance is level. What does this show?

options.A: The stone is heavier because it is smaller.
options.C: The box is heavier because it is bigger.

questions.explanation: A level balance shows equal mass. Size alone does not tell us the mass.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A wide bowl and a tall jar each hold exactly 4 of the same cupfuls when full. What is true?

options.B: The bowl holds more because it is wider.
options.C: The jar holds more because it is taller.

questions.explanation: Both hold the same number of equal cupfuls, so their capacities are equal.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Three races start together. The red car stops first, the blue car stops next, and the green car stops last. Put the colours in order from shortest to longest moving time.
questions.explanation: With the same start, the first car to stop moves for the shortest time.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept the three colours or car names in this order.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A book and a drawer are in different rooms. How could you compare their lengths?

options.B: Use string to copy the book’s length, then compare the string with the drawer’s length.

questions.answer: Use string to copy the book’s length, then compare the string with the drawer’s length.
questions.explanation: A piece of string can carry the book’s length to the drawer for an indirect comparison.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A toy and 3 equal blocks balance. A ball and 5 of the same blocks balance. Which is heavier?
questions.explanation: The ball balances more of the same blocks, so it is heavier.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Container A holds more than B. Container C holds more than A. Which holds the most?
questions.explanation: C holds more than A, and A holds more than B.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two songs start together. Song A is still playing after song B ends. Which song is longer? Give a reason.
questions.answer: Song A, because it keeps playing after song B ends.
questions.explanation: When two songs start together, the one that ends later lasts longer.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept A with a reason referring to its later finish or continued playing.
questions.correct_answer: Song A, because it keeps playing after song B ends.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two sticks lie on a table with their starting ends in different places. How can you compare their lengths fairly?

options.A: Move the shorter-looking stick further forward.
options.B: Line up one end of each stick.

questions.answer: Line up one end of each stick.
questions.explanation: Lining up the starting ends lets you compare how far each stick reaches.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A teddy and a bag balance. The bag is heavier than a ball. Which is heavier: the teddy or the ball?
questions.explanation: The teddy has the same mass as the bag. The bag is heavier than the ball, so the teddy is too.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A full bottle exactly fills an empty jug, with no water left over. What can you say?

options.A: The bottle and jug have the same capacity.
options.B: The jug has a greater capacity.
options.C: The bottle has a greater capacity.

questions.answer: The bottle and jug have the same capacity.
questions.explanation: An exact transfer with no space or water left over shows equal capacities.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Ribbon A is shorter than ribbon B. Ribbon C is longer than ribbon B. Write the ribbons from shortest to longest.
questions.explanation: A is shorter than B, and C is longer than B.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept ribbon names in this order.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two paper spinners start and stop together. What is true about their spinning times?

options.A: The larger spinner spins for longer.
options.B: The smaller spinner spins for longer.
options.C: They spin for the same time.

questions.answer: They spin for the same time.
questions.explanation: The same start and the same finish mean the spinning times are equal.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A rope reaches further than a stick when one end of each is lined up. Why is the rope longer?

options.B: Its far end reaches beyond the stick’s far end.
options.C: It is softer than the stick.

questions.answer: Its far end reaches beyond the stick’s far end.
questions.explanation: Length is compared by how far each object reaches from the same start.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: You pour water from a full cup into an empty pot. The pot fills while some water is still in the cup. Which holds less?
questions.explanation: The pot fills before all the cup’s water has been used, so it holds less.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: You have two bags and a balance. How could you find which bag is heavier?
questions.answer: Put one bag on each side of the balance. The side that goes down has the heavier bag.
questions.explanation: A balance compares mass directly. A level balance would show that the bags have the same mass.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept placing a bag on each side and identifying the lower side as heavier; mentioning equal mass is optional.
questions.correct_answer: Put one bag on each side of the balance. The side that goes down has the heavier bag.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two straws start at the same line. Straw X reaches further than straw Y. Which is shorter?
questions.explanation: With one end lined up, the straw that does not reach as far is shorter.

visual.caption: Both objects start at the same place. Each block is the same length.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A balance has a toy boat and a toy train. The train side is lower. What is true?
questions.explanation: The lower side of a balance holds the heavier object.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question:
The same cup is used to fill three empty containers.
A: 2 cupfuls
B: 6 cupfuls
C: 4 cupfuls
Which order goes from least to greatest capacity?
questions.explanation: Fewer equal cupfuls means a smaller capacity: 2, then 4, then 6.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A walk and a game begin together. The walk ends while the game is still going. Which activity lasts longer?
questions.explanation: The game continues after the walk ends, although they began together.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept game.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A string is the same length as a brush. A pencil is shorter than the string. Which is longer: the brush or the pencil?
questions.explanation: The brush matches the string, and the pencil is shorter than the string.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Bag A balances 2 equal blocks. Bag B balances 4 of the same blocks. Bag C balances 3 of them. Which bag is lightest?
questions.explanation: Bag A balances the fewest of the same blocks.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A full jug is poured into an empty bucket. All the water fits, and the bucket still has room. Why does the bucket have a greater capacity?

options.A: It can hold the jug’s water and more.
options.C: It must be a different colour.

questions.answer: It can hold the jug’s water and more.
questions.explanation: The unused space shows that the bucket can hold more water than the jug.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Three children start building at the same time. Lee finishes first, Pat finishes second, and Ari finishes last. Who spends the longest time building?
questions.explanation: With the same start, the last person to finish spends the longest time building.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept Ari.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A box looks bigger than a parcel. How can you check which has more mass?

options.C: Put them on opposite sides of a balance.

questions.answer: Put them on opposite sides of a balance.
questions.explanation: A balance compares mass. A bigger size does not always mean more mass.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A ribbon is longer than a spoon. The spoon is longer than a key. Which statement must be true?

options.A: The ribbon and key have equal lengths.
options.B: The ribbon is longer than the key.
options.C: The key is longer than the ribbon.

questions.answer: The ribbon is longer than the key.
questions.explanation: The ribbon is longer than the spoon, which is already longer than the key.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A bowl takes 3 full cups to fill. A pot takes 3 full mugs. The cups and mugs have different sizes. Can you tell which container holds more from these counts?

options.A: Yes, the bowl must hold more.
options.B: No, the measuring containers are different sizes.
options.C: Yes, they must hold the same amount.

questions.answer: No, the measuring containers are different sizes.
questions.explanation: The same count does not show equal capacity when the cupfuls have different sizes.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two timers start together and ring together. Compare the times they measured.
questions.explanation: Matching starts and finishes show equal durations.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept equal times or same duration.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A toy is heavier than a sock but lighter than a book. Which order is from heaviest to lightest?
questions.explanation: The book is heaviest, then the toy, then the sock.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: You want to compare the widths of two doors in different rooms. What could help?

options.A: Open both doors and guess from their sounds.
options.C: Use a string to copy one width and compare it with the other.

questions.answer: Use a string to copy one width and compare it with the other.
questions.explanation: String can carry one door’s width to the other door for an indirect comparison.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: Two songs start together. A child says, “Song A is longer because it is louder.” What would actually show that A lasts longer?

options.A: A is still playing when B ends.
options.C: A is sung by more people.

questions.answer: A is still playing when B ends.
questions.explanation: The later finish shows a longer duration when both songs start together.

questions.skill_title: Comparing Length, Mass, Capacity and Duration
questions.question: A full can exactly fills an empty bowl. No water spills and none is left in the can. Compare their capacities and explain.
questions.answer: They have the same capacity because the can’s water exactly fills the bowl.
questions.explanation: The exact transfer shows that both containers hold the same amount when full.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept equal/same capacity with a reason about exactly filling the bowl.
questions.correct_answer: They have the same capacity because the can’s water exactly fills the bowl.

questions.question: A strip is covered from end to end by 4 equal blocks. There are no gaps or overlaps. How long is the strip?
questions.explanation: Each block is one length unit. Four blocks cover the strip exactly.

visual.caption: Four equal blocks cover the strip with no gaps or overlaps.

questions.question: Which objects would make fair length units?

options.B: A mix of big and small buttons

questions.explanation: Equal-size units let each count stand for the same length.

questions.question: A pencil is measured with equal cubes. Small gaps are left between the cubes. What should change?

options.C: Move the cubes together so they touch.

questions.answer: Move the cubes together so they touch.
questions.explanation: Length units should touch end to end, without gaps.

questions.question: Six equal tiles cover a ribbon exactly. The tiles touch with no gaps or overlaps. How long is the ribbon in tiles?
questions.explanation: Count one unit for each tile that covers the ribbon.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 6 or six tiles.

visual.caption: 6 equal units cover the whole length, touching end to end.

questions.question:
A leaf matches this row of equal blocks exactly. The blocks touch end to end.
Leaf: □ □ □ □ □ □
How many blocks long is the leaf?
questions.explanation: Count the six equal blocks that cover the leaf from one end to the other.

visual.caption: Each block is one equal length unit. The row matches the whole leaf.

questions.question:
The same blocks measure two strips exactly.
Strip A: 5 blocks
Strip B: 8 blocks
Which strip is longer?
questions.explanation: More of the same length unit means a longer strip.

questions.question: Paper clips overlap along a bookmark. What is the best way to fix the measure?

options.A: Push the clips further over each other.
options.C: Place the clips end to end without overlapping.

questions.answer: Place the clips end to end without overlapping.
questions.explanation: Overlapping units cover some parts twice. Place them end to end to measure fairly.

questions.question: Four cubes cover part of a stick. Two more of the same cubes are needed to reach its end. All cubes will touch. How many cubes long is the stick?
questions.explanation: Four cubes and two more cubes cover the whole stick.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 6 or six cubes.

questions.question: A strip is measured once with short blocks and once with long blocks. The blocks always touch and cover it exactly. Which measure uses more blocks?

options.C: Both must use the same number.

questions.explanation: More short units are needed to cover the same length.

questions.question:
A line matches this row of equal matchsticks. They touch end to end.
Line: — — — — — — —
Which label gives its length?
questions.explanation: There are seven matchsticks in the row. Record both the count and the unit name.

visual.caption: Each block represents one equal matchstick laid end to end.

questions.question: A leaf is covered by 3 long blocks and 2 short blocks. Why is “5 blocks long” not a fair measure in equal units?
questions.explanation: Each length unit must have the same size for the count to be a fair measure.

questions.question: A cord is 8 cubes long. A straw is 5 of the same cubes long. How many cubes longer is the cord?
questions.explanation: The cord has 3 more equal cube lengths than the straw.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 3 or three cubes.

questions.question:
Each □ is one equal cube. All cubes touch.
A: □ □ □
B: □ □ □ □ □
C: □ □ □ □ □ □
Which row makes a path exactly 5 cubes long?
questions.explanation: Row B has five equal cubes. Their joined lengths make a path five cubes long.

visual.caption: One block represents one equal cube. Cubes touch end to end.

questions.question:
The same cubes are used for every measure.
Brush: 6 cubes
Spoon: 4 cubes
Comb: 5 cubes
Which order is shortest to longest?
questions.explanation: Compare the counts of the same unit: 4, then 5, then 6.

questions.question:
A ribbon matches this row of equal blocks.
Ribbon: □ □ □ □ □
Jo counts the joins and says it is 4 blocks long. What is the correct length?
questions.explanation: There are five blocks, although there are only four joins between them. Count the blocks as the units.

visual.caption: Equal blocks touch end to end and match the whole ribbon. Count the blocks, not the joins.

questions.question: Make a strip 5 tiles long using equal tiles. How should you place the tiles?
questions.answer: Place 5 equal tiles end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
questions.explanation: The tiles need to form one continuous length, each unit used once.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept five tiles touching end to end, without gaps or overlaps.
questions.correct_answer: Place 5 equal tiles end to end with no gaps or overlaps.

questions.question: A child measures a desk with a big handspan, then with a small handspan. Why might the counts differ?

options.B: One count must always be wrong.

questions.explanation: Different-size units can give different counts for the same length.

questions.question: A card is exactly 4 blocks long. Each block is 2 cubes long. How many cubes would cover the card end to end?
questions.explanation: Each block length is replaced by 2 cubes: 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.question:
The same blocks measure two ribbons exactly.
A: □ □ □ □ □ □
B: □ □ □ □ □ □ □ □
How long is the shorter ribbon?
questions.explanation: Ribbon A uses six blocks and ribbon B uses eight. The shorter ribbon is six blocks long.

visual.caption: Equal blocks touch end to end and cover each whole ribbon.

questions.question: A tray is 7 equal blocks long. A row of blocks on the tray is only 5 blocks long. How many more matching blocks will complete the row?
questions.explanation: Two more blocks extend the row from 5 blocks to 7 blocks.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 2 or two blocks.

questions.question: Two ribbons are each exactly 6 of the same paper clips long. What is true?
questions.explanation: Equal counts of the same unit show equal lengths.

questions.question:
Each □ is one equal block.
A: □ □ □
B: □ □ □ □ □
C: □ □ □ □ □ □
Which strip is 2 blocks longer than A?
questions.explanation: A is three blocks long. B has two extra blocks, so it is five blocks long.

visual.caption: Equal blocks touch end to end and show each strip’s whole length.

questions.question: A strip ends halfway along the fifth block. The first four blocks fit fully. What is the best description?

options.A: More than 4 blocks but less than 5 blocks long

questions.answer: More than 4 blocks but less than 5 blocks long
questions.explanation: Four whole blocks are not enough, but five whole blocks go past the end.

questions.question: A line was measured with cubes, but some cubes overlapped. Explain how to measure it again fairly.
questions.answer: Use equal cubes, start at one end, and place them end to end with no gaps or overlaps. Count the cubes.
questions.explanation: A fair measure covers the length once with equal units.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept equal units placed from one end to the other without overlaps or gaps, then counted.
questions.correct_answer: Use equal cubes, start at one end, and place them end to end with no gaps or overlaps. Count the cubes.

questions.question: Five equal paper clips touch end to end and match a strip exactly. How long is the strip?
questions.explanation: There is one unit for each of the five paper clips.

visual.caption: 5 equal units cover the whole length, touching end to end.

questions.question:
Each □ is one equal tile. The rows match the whole lengths of the objects.
Tray: □ □ □ □
Mat: □ □ □ □ □ □
Which object is 6 tiles long?
questions.explanation: Six equal tiles cover the mat. The tray is only four tiles long.

visual.caption: Each block is one equal tile. Tiles touch end to end.

questions.question:
The same tiles measure three lines.
A: 9 tiles
B: 6 tiles
C: 7 tiles
Which line is shortest?
questions.explanation: Six is the smallest count of the same unit, so B is shortest.

questions.question: A brush is 7 cubes long. A crayon is 4 of the same cubes long. How many cubes shorter is the crayon?
questions.explanation: The difference between 7 and 4 equal cube lengths is 3.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 3 or three cubes.

questions.question: A child leaves gaps between the blocks used to measure a shelf. Why is the count unreliable?

options.B: The blocks are all the same size.
options.C: Some shelf length is covered by gaps instead of blocks.

questions.answer: Some shelf length is covered by gaps instead of blocks.
questions.explanation: The gaps add length that has not been counted as units.

questions.question:
Equal blocks measure three strips. Each row matches the whole strip.
A: □ □ □ □ □
B: □ □ □ □ □ □ □
C: □ □ □ □ □
Which pair has equal lengths?
questions.explanation: A and C each measure five of the same blocks, so their lengths are equal.

visual.caption: Equal blocks touch end to end and cover each whole strip.

questions.question: A strip uses 10 short clips or 5 long clips when measured correctly. Which clips are longer?

options.A: The clips used in the group of 5
options.B: The clips used in the group of 10

questions.answer: The clips used in the group of 5
questions.explanation: Fewer units cover the same strip when each unit is longer.

questions.question: Equal blocks cover a ribbon exactly. There are 8 blocks and 7 joins between them. Record the ribbon’s length with its unit.
questions.explanation: The blocks are the length units; the joins are not extra units.
questions.acceptance_note: Require 8 and blocks.

questions.question: A child starts measuring a stick one cube-length after its end. What has been missed?

options.B: An extra cube beyond the stick
options.C: The first part of the stick

questions.answer: The first part of the stick
questions.explanation: Starting after the end leaves part of the whole length unmeasured.

questions.question: A ribbon is 6 beads long. Another ribbon is 6 beads long. The bead sizes are not given. Must the ribbons have equal lengths?

options.A: No, because two ribbons can never match.
options.C: No, the beads might have different lengths.

questions.answer: No, the beads might have different lengths.
questions.explanation: Equal counts show equal lengths only when the length units match.

questions.question: A line is covered exactly by 3 equal sticks. Each stick is as long as 2 equal tiles. How many tiles long is the line?
questions.explanation: Each stick is replaced by 2 tiles: 2, 4, 6.

questions.question: A strip is 9 cubes long. So far, 6 matching cubes have been placed correctly along it. How many more are needed?
questions.explanation: Three more cubes complete the length from 6 to 9 cubes.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 3 or three cubes.

questions.question: Equal blocks cover a card, but two blocks overlap. What should you do?

options.A: Count the overlap as an extra block.
options.B: Keep the overlap and use the same count.
options.C: Spread them end to end, then measure and count again.

questions.answer: Spread them end to end, then measure and count again.
questions.explanation: Overlaps cover a part twice. Arrange units correctly before recording the count.

questions.question: A rope is 8 tiles long and a cord is 8 of the same tiles long. Which statement is true?

options.A: The cord is shorter because it is a cord.
options.C: The rope is longer because it is a rope.

questions.explanation: Matching counts of the same length unit show equal lengths.

questions.question: Six whole blocks fit along a strip. The strip continues partway along a seventh block. Which description fits?

options.A: More than 6 and less than 7 blocks long

questions.answer: More than 6 and less than 7 blocks long
questions.explanation: The strip is longer than six full units but does not reach seven full units.

questions.question: You must make a path exactly 6 equal tiles long. Describe how you will place and check the tiles.
questions.answer: Place 6 equal tiles end to end with no gaps or overlaps, then count them.
questions.explanation: The whole path is made from six equal length units that touch.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept six matching tiles touching end to end, with a count/check of six.
questions.correct_answer: Place 6 equal tiles end to end with no gaps or overlaps, then count them.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Which unit best describes the time from one birthday to the next birthday?
questions.explanation: A birthday comes around once each year.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A week has 7 days. Which is longer: one day or one week?
questions.explanation: A week contains seven days, so it is longer than one day.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The days go Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Which day comes just after Tuesday?
questions.explanation: Wednesday follows Tuesday.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Put these parts of one day in order: evening, morning, afternoon.
questions.explanation: Morning comes first, then afternoon, then evening.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept the three words in this order.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A year has 12 months. Which is longer?
questions.explanation: A year includes twelve months.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The school day goes: arrive, read, eat lunch, go home. What happens just before lunch?
questions.explanation: Reading is immediately before lunch in the given sequence.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A school assembly lasts about one _____. Choose a sensible unit.
questions.explanation: An hour is a sensible time for an assembly. A month or a year would be far too long.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The months go January, February, March, April. Which month is between February and April?
questions.explanation: March comes after February and before April.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept March.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A class watches a seed grow for 3 weeks. A painting session lasts 1 hour. Which takes longer?
questions.explanation: Three weeks is much longer than one hour.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The days go Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday. What comes just after Sunday?
questions.explanation: The weekly sequence continues to Monday after Sunday.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Which unit is most useful for saying how old a Year 1 child is?
questions.explanation: Children’s ages are usually described in years.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A week has 7 days. A camp lasts one whole week. How many days is that?
questions.explanation: One week and seven days describe the same duration.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept 7 or seven days.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The months go May, June, July. A class trip is in June and a concert is in July. Which event comes first?

options.C: They are in the same month.

questions.explanation: June comes before July.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Mila reads for 1 hour. Ben builds for 2 hours. Who spends less time on the activity?
questions.explanation: One hour is less time than two hours.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: The plan is: plant a seed, water it, watch it grow. Which event is last?
questions.explanation: Watching it grow is the last event in the given plan.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Put these durations in order from shortest to longest: 1 week, 1 hour, 1 day.
questions.explanation: An hour is shorter than a day, and a day is shorter than a week.
questions.acceptance_note: Accept hour, day, week in this order.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question:
The class has music on the 10th. Use this calendar row.
Monday: 8
Tuesday: 9
Wednesday: 10
Thursday: 11
Friday: 12
What day is music?
questions.explanation: The date 10 is in the Wednesday column.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: Today is Thursday. Yesterday was Wednesday. Which day was earlier?
questions.explanation: Yesterday is the day before today.

questions.skill_title: Time: Years, Months, Weeks, Days and Hours
questions.question: A building project takes 2 years. A garden project takes 2 months. Which is shorter?
